Can a squatter take ownership of a Vermont house?

In theory, yes. Vermont recognizes adverse possession, so a person who occupies land in the right way for the full statutory period can ask a court to recognize title. The period is 15 years, and the claim is hard to win.

The 15-year number comes from the limitations statute for suing to recover land. 12 V.S.A. 501 requires an action for the recovery of lands, or the possession of them, to be commenced within 15 years after the cause of action first accrues to the plaintiff, with an exception for cases covered by 32 V.S.A. 5263. If the true owner never sues inside that window, the occupier's position can ripen into title.

Most people searching for Vermont squatters rights are asking about one of three situations. Someone is living in a house the owner doesn't control. A neighbor has used part of a lot for decades. Or a former tenant won't leave. Vermont law treats these differently, and the right fix depends on which one you have.

What an occupier must prove

The occupier carries the burden of proof on every element. In Mahoney v. Tara, LLC, 2014 VT 90, the Vermont Supreme Court held that the claimant must show use or possession of the disputed land in an open, notorious, hostile and continuous manner for the full fifteen-year period.

The fifteen years is part of the claimant's own case, not a defense the title owner has to raise. The court also described adverse possession as a common-law claim for recognition of title, so a court is confirming something that already happened, not creating new rights.

ElementWhat it asksWhat it means for an owner
OpenUse that anyone could seeRegular visits to the lot, even occasional, give you the chance to notice and object
NotoriousUse that is known in the communityNeighbors and town officials may be able to say who has been using the land
HostileUse without the owner's permissionA written permission or a lease can cut against this element
ContinuousUse through the full 15 yearsGaps in use can break the period

How the 15-year clock works and what stops it

The clock stops when the title owner brings a claim, not when the occupier does. Mahoney held that only a title owner's claim against the possessor tolls the period. The possessor's own suit to quiet title doesn't.

In that case, the owner's motion to dismiss, which asserted ownership and gave the other side adequate notice, tolled the period in January 2008 before fifteen years had run. The trial court had added two separate stretches of possession that together came to less than thirteen years. The Supreme Court left open whether adding them together was proper, because it resolved the case on tolling.

The practical lesson is simple. If you find a stranger on your land, write down the date you first learned of it, and act in writing. Silence for a decade or more is what gives these claims their force.

Removing someone who has no right to be there

Vermont uses a court process called ejectment, and an owner who wins gets a writ of possession. Chapter 169 of Title 12 sets out the steps, and the Superior Court handles the case.

  • Under 12 V.S.A. 4854, a winning plaintiff receives judgment for possession, rents due, damages and costs. Attorney's fees may be added if a written rental agreement allows them.
  • The writ issues on the judgment date unless the court stays it for good cause.
  • The sheriff serves the writ and may not put the plaintiff in possession earlier than 14 days after service.
  • Under section 4854a, a landlord may dispose of belongings left behind without notice or liability 15 days after the writ is served or possession is restored, whichever is later.

Self-help is a poor idea. For tenants, 9 V.S.A. 4463 bars a landlord from cutting off utilities, locking the tenant out or withholding the tenant's belongings except through proper judicial process. A landlord may not remove a tenant without a court order.

What if the occupant is a tenant or subtenant?

A tenant who stays past the end of a lease is not a squatter in the adverse possession sense, because the stay began with the owner's permission. The owner uses the eviction route instead.

  • Give written notice that states the grounds and a termination date. Delivery can be by hand, first-class mail to the last known address, or certified mail.
  • Wait until the termination date passes, then file within 60 days or send a new notice.
  • File the complaint for ejectment in the Civil Division of the Superior Court in the county where the property sits, with the lease and the notice attached.
  • Arrange for a sheriff or constable to serve the papers. The tenant generally has 21 days after service to answer.
  • If the landlord wins, the sheriff serves the writ. The tenant generally has 14 days to leave, or 7 days if the case rests on a missed rent escrow payment.

Section 4853b adds a faster track for an unlawful occupant who has no right or permission to be in a unit where the lease bars subleasing. The hearing comes after 10 days' notice, and a writ lets the sheriff act not sooner than five days after service. The defendant can still oppose by showing a genuine dispute of fact.

For a true stranger in the house, the court's Access and Resource Center and VTLawHelp are the places to ask for guidance.

Betterments in an ejectment case

Betterments are a counterclaim for the value of improvements an occupier made to land they honestly thought they owned. Under 12 V.S.A. 4811, the defendant in an ejectment action asserts it, and recovery depends on the owner winning the ejectment claim.

The value is measured by how much the improvements increased the land's value. The defendant, or someone the defendant claims under, must have bought the land believing the title to be good or taken a lease believing it conveyed the interest it described.

A long-running dispute over a rebuilt garage, a new septic system or a barn can add a money claim on top of the title question, and a buyer who inherits the problem inherits the claim too.

Before you sell with an occupant or boundary question

Clear the occupancy or boundary issue first, or sell to a buyer who will take the house as it stands. Unresolved possession claims make a sale harder, and a deed has to meet Vermont's formal requirements to be recorded.

Under 27 V.S.A. 341, a deed must be signed by the grantor, acknowledged before a notary public and recorded in the land records of the town where the land lies. If the deed refers to a survey made or revised after July 1, 1988, the survey must accompany it or be cited by volume and page. Conveyances after January 1, 2020 that subdivide a parcel or change its boundaries need a plat or a citation to one.

Transfer tax at closing

Property transfer tax is payable within 30 days of closing. The general rate is 1.25% plus a 0.22% clean water surcharge. A principal residence pays 0.5% on the first $200,000 and 1.47% above that. A non-principal home fit for year-round use that is not a long-term rental pays 3.40%, or 3.62% with the surcharge. Because the rate depends on how the property is used, confirm it with the Department of Taxes before closing.

If you own a Vermont house with a squatter, a tenant who won't leave or an inherited property no one has visited, a cash buyer can purchase as-is. We don't give legal advice, and an attorney should review any title question before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Can a squatter claim my Vermont house after a few years?

No. Vermont uses a 15-year period under 12 V.S.A. 501, and the occupier must prove open, notorious, hostile and continuous use for all of it. A few years of occupancy doesn't meet that standard.

Do I need a court order to remove someone from my Vermont property?

Yes, if the person is a tenant, and in practice for any occupant who refuses to leave. Vermont law bars landlords from lockouts and utility shutoffs outside proper judicial process, and a writ of possession is served by the sheriff.

How long after a Vermont eviction judgment does the occupant have to leave?

Generally 14 days after the sheriff serves the writ of possession under 12 V.S.A. 4854. A missed rent escrow payment shortens that to 7 days, and the unlawful occupant track in section 4853b uses five days.

Does giving permission stop an adverse possession claim?

Permission cuts against the hostile element, because the use is no longer against the owner's rights. Written permission, a lease or a signed license is easier to prove later than a verbal okay.

Who pays Vermont property transfer tax when I sell?

Payment is due within 30 days of the closing date, and the rate depends on how the property is used.

What happens to tenants when a Vermont landlord sells

A sale does not end a tenancy in Vermont on its own. The landlord still needs a legal reason and a written notice. Residential rental law sits in Title 9, Chapter 137 of the Vermont Statutes.

One provision speaks to a sale directly: 9 V.S.A. § 4467(d). A landlord who has contracted to sell the building may end a tenancy with no written rental agreement on at least 30 days of actual notice.

Security deposits travel with the property. When the landlord's interest ends, the deposit goes to the new landlord, who must give the tenant actual notice of the new landlord's name and address (9 V.S.A. § 4461(f)).

How much notice a Vermont landlord must give

The notice period turns on the reason and on whether there is a written lease. Section 4467 sets these periods.

SituationNotice
Nonpayment of rent14 days
Breach of a material lease term30 days before the termination date
Criminal, drug or violent activity that threatens other residents14 days
No written agreement, monthly rent, tenant of two years or less60 days
No written agreement, monthly rent, tenant of more than two years90 days
No written agreement, weekly rent21 days
No written agreement, landlord has contracted to sell the building30 days
Written lease, no-cause ending, tenant of two years or less30 days before the end of the stated term
Written lease, no-cause ending, tenant of more than two years60 days before the end of the stated term

The notice has to state the termination date. An eviction case must be filed within 60 days of that date, or the notice can't support a judgment. Taking rent after termination generally doesn't waive the landlord's remedies for breach or no-cause termination, and taking partial rent doesn't waive remedies for nonpayment.

Lock changes and utility shutoffs

A landlord can't use self-help to speed up a sale. Under 9 V.S.A. § 4463, removing a tenant, changing the locks, shutting off utilities or removing belongings all require a court order.

Written notice can be delivered by hand, by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address, or by certified mail. Some towns require more notice than the statute, and subsidized rentals such as Section 8 carry extra requirements, so check the lease and any program rules.

The Vermont eviction process

Vermont calls an eviction ejectment. It is filed in the Civil Division of the Superior Court in the county where the property sits, and it moves in these steps.

  1. Serve a written termination notice with the grounds and the termination date.
  2. Wait until the date passes, then file within 60 days with the complaint, a copy of the lease if written, the notice, and the CARES Act declaration (form 100-00031).
  3. A sheriff or constable serves the tenant, and the landlord files the return of service.
  4. The tenant generally has 21 days after service to file a written answer. With no answer, the landlord may seek a default judgment.
  5. A judge decides at hearing or trial whether the tenant can be evicted and whether either side owes money.
  6. If the landlord wins, the court issues a writ of possession, and the tenant has 14 days after service to leave.

A landlord can ask the court to order past-due rent paid into escrow while the case is pending (12 V.S.A. § 4853a). If the tenant misses a payment, the landlord is entitled to immediate possession and the tenant must leave within 7 days. A writ stays effective for 60 days after it issues, and the landlord may dispose of remaining belongings on the later of 15 days after the writ is served or the date the landlord legally retakes possession.

A buyer who wants vacant possession may have to wait for a case to run its course. Either side may appeal legal errors to the Vermont Supreme Court.

A tenant's rights while the landlord is trying to sell

Listing the house changes nothing for the tenant. The implied warranty of habitability, protection from retaliation, and the rules on rent increases and deposits all still apply.

  • Habitability, 9 V.S.A. § 4457: the landlord is treated as promising premises that are safe, clean and fit for human habitation, and a rental agreement can't waive that promise. The unit needs heat that can safely provide a reasonable amount of warmth, and adequate water with hot and cold lines.
  • Retaliation, § 4465: a landlord may not retaliate against a tenant who complains to a government agency about a health or safety violation, complains to the landlord about a violation, or joins a tenant group. A termination notice within 90 days of a municipal or state violation notice, for reasons other than unpaid rent, is presumed retaliatory.
  • Rent, § 4455: rent is due without demand, and an increase takes effect on the first day of the next rental period after at least 60 days of actual notice.
  • Tenant conduct, § 4456: a tenant must not damage the premises or interfere with other tenants' peaceful enjoyment, and can end a tenancy by giving actual notice at least one rental payment period before the termination date unless the lease says otherwise.

A landlord who files a notice to sell soon after a code complaint should expect the retaliation presumption to come up.

Security deposit rules

The deposit and a written itemized statement are due within 14 days after the landlord learns the tenant has moved out or abandoned the unit, or after the move-out date if the tenant gave notice. Seasonal rentals that aren't a primary residence get 60 days.

A landlord may keep money only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other charges owed, and removal of abandoned articles. Miss the 14 days and the right to withhold any part is lost. A willful failure makes the landlord liable for double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees and costs. A tenant owed a deposit can use small claims court for up to $10,000, and Brattleboro and Burlington have additional deposit rules.

If you're selling, an accurate deposit ledger belongs in the closing package, because the buyer takes over the duty to return each deposit.

Rental inspections and the health and safety code

The Division of Fire Safety, within the Department of Public Safety, is the primary enforcer of the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code under Act 181, signed June 7, 2022. The program took effect January 1, 2024. Local health officials keep concurrent authority and can still inspect.

The program runs on complaints. Tenants first contact the owner or manager, and if that fails they can submit an online complaint form that routes to the regional office for the property's ZIP code. The Division has regional offices in Williston, Waterbury, Rutland and Springfield. Short-term rentals count as rentals, but the Division inspects them only in response to complaints.

Taxes and reporting when selling a Vermont rental

Landlords who rent residential property for 30 or more days in a row file a Landlord Certificate (Form LRC-140) with the Department of Taxes each year for each property with a rented unit. A landlord who skips the filing may be fined, with interest.

On the sale itself, property transfer tax is 1.25 percent for a year-round home that is a long-term rental, and 3.40 percent for a non-principal residence fit for year-round habitation that is not a long-term rental. The 0.22 percent Clean Water Surcharge is added in both cases, so ask your attorney which category your building falls into. Under 32 V.S.A. § 9602 the Commissioner may assess the higher rate if a landlord certificate is filed without a real landlord-tenant relationship.

A nonresident landlord should expect 2.5 percent withholding on the sale price, reported by the buyer on Form RW-171 within 30 days, unless a Commissioner's Certificate is obtained.

Where landlords and tenants can get help

Three places to start: the Access and Resource Center at 802-879-1185 or selfhelp@vtcourts.gov, the CVOEO tenant hotline at 802-864-0099, and Vermont Legal Aid at 800-889-2047.

Cases are filed in the county where the rental sits. If you are weighing a sale instead of a long eviction or a costly repair, an as-is cash offer from Cash Home Buyers is one option to compare.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Vermont landlord end a tenancy because the house is being sold?

Only with proper notice. If there is no written agreement and the landlord has contracted to sell the building, 9 V.S.A. § 4467(d) allows at least 30 days of actual notice.

How many days does a landlord have to return a security deposit in Vermont?

14 days after learning the tenant moved out, or after the move-out date if notice was given, with an itemized written statement. Seasonal rentals get 60 days.

How much notice is needed for nonpayment of rent?

14 days under 9 V.S.A. § 4467(a). A written lease doesn't lengthen it.

Can a Vermont landlord remove a tenant without going to court?

No. Removing a tenant, changing locks, shutting off utilities or removing belongings all require a court order.

How long does a tenant have to leave after a writ of possession?

14 days after service of the writ, or 7 days after a missed rent escrow payment.
